Source: http://www.norml.org

Posted March 6, 2000
Report on the CASA Conference - Mar 1-3, 2000 - Reagan Library, Simi Valley
by Dale Gieringer, Cal. NORML

A VISIT TO THE BELLY OF THE BEAST

The Center for Addiction and Substance Abuse (CASA), Joe Califano's anti-drug think tank, held a conference at the Reagan Library in Simi Valley, Cal. last week. Seeing as how the agenda included a couple of spokesmen from our side, including former Baltimore mayor Kurt Schmoke, who was scheduled to debate ex-Drug-Czar William Bennett, a small delegation of us decided to attend (Ventura County Prop. 215 patient Lisa Schwarz ,
myself, and two others).

The conference, entitled " Substance Abuse in the 21st Century, " featured a stellar lineup of fearsome drug warriors from the last century, including former Attorney General Ed Meese, former Bush, Sr. drug advisor Dr. Herbert Kleber, Partnership for a Drug-Free America Chairman James Burke, NIDA Director Alan Leshner, Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey, and Nancy Reagan herself, whose presence was repeatedly greeted by standing ovations from everyone but ourselves.

A panel on " Law, Order and Substance Abuse, " moderated by Califano, featured a panel of hard-line legalists, including criminology Prof. James Q. Wilson, former NYPD Comnissioner William J. Bratton, Ed Meese, and DEA District Administrator Michelle Lenhart, plus one moderate, Drug Court Judge Rudolf Diaz of El Monte, Cal. The panelists uniformly pronounced themselves in favor of stricter measures - most notably drug testing – to force drug users into treatment. However, Judge Diaz got a scattering of applause when he noted that massive incarceration of users raised " moral questions. "

Califano did not see fit to turn the discussion to the issue of America's record number of drug prisoners. a matter that was hardly mentioned at the entire conference except in a flyer that we handed out to interested attendees. However, most of the panelists, including the DEA spokesperson, admitted there were problems with mandatory minimum drug sentences. Even Prof. Wilson, a strong mandatory minimum proponent, pronounced the crack/cocaine disparity to be " grossly unjustified. "

Commissioner Bratton turned out to be surprisingly thoughtful, warning that the U.S. was " addicted " to the notion that police can handle the problem of drug control. He also attacked " Three Strikes " and mandatory minimums, and insisted that good policing should not compromise civil liberties protections such as Miranda warnings.

We were angered to hear the DEA spokesperson attack California's Prop. 215 for sending a harmful message to children, but none of us were able to get the floor during the Q&A period to set the record straight.

SCHMOKE-BENNETT DEBATE

The dinner debate between Schmoke and Bennett, which was broadcast on CSPAN, broke no new ground. Schmoke ably articulated his position that drugs should be primarily a health, not law enforcement, concern. Bennett huffed and blustered, calling for a " restoration of moral authority to this issue " and crowing about the wonderful accomplishments of his own tenure (under which, it will be recalled, our cities were wracked by unprecedented drug-prohibition-related violence).

Descending into obscene boorishness, Bennett compared legalized drugs to legalized rape, then joked about " medical rape. " This prompted a walk-out by Craig Schwarz, husband of medical marijuana patient and Prop. 215 defendant Lisa Schwarz, who was herself unable to attend the dinner due to a migraine attack.

Schmoke won a round by forcing Bennett to admit that tobacco prohibition was a bad idea in view of the enormous enforcement problems it would generate. " People can have fun drinking, they can have fun smoking, " Bennett generously proclaimed - but the second half of his statement provoked a chorus of guffaws from the audience.

SECOND CONFERENCE DAY

A panel on drug treatment offered an opportunity to inject a drug reform proposal into the debate. Panelists included Dr. Alan Leshner, whom Califano praised as having ushered in the " Golden Era of NIDA, " Dr. Herbert Kleber, a former crony of William Bennett at ONDCP, and Charles Hynes, a Brooklyn D.A. who promotes treatment diversion programs.

Kleber, Leshner, and Hynes all bewailed the lack of federal funding for treatment, complaining that legislators lacked the political will to fund anything other than enforcement.

I had a chance to follow up on this during the Q&A. Holding up a copy of the California Substance Abuse and Crime Prevention initiative, I explained that there was an initiative circulating in California which would fund drug treatment diversion programs to the tune of $120 million, and that it would save the state money by eliminating imprisonment for non-violent drug possession offenders.

I asked whether this initiative might not address the problems deplored by the panel. An embarrassed silence followed. Leshner ventured that this was outside his policy area.

At last, Kleber and Hynes muttered that it would depend on the details of the proposal. Other conference attendees later asked me for copies of the initiative.

The media highlight of the conference was a panel on legal drugs, featuring an exchange on tobacco between former FDA commissioner David Kessler and the Senior Vice-President of Philip Morris, Steven Parrish. Parrish made news by announcing that his company now supports " serious regulation of tobacco at the federal level. " However, he differed sharply from Kessler in insisting that new Congressional legislation is needed on the grounds that tobacco is presently not under FDA's authority (an issue now being litigated before the Supreme Court). Kessler expressed hope and skepticism over Philip Morris' change of heart. He insisted on the ultimate goal that tobacco should cease to be seen as a " socially acceptable product. " Asked whether he had ever entertained the possibility that any of his ideas might be wrong,, Kessler humorlessly failed to answer the question.

The most stirring debate at the conference was a discussion of drug testing moderated by Sander Vanocur. pitting ACLU President Nadine Strossen and former Treasury Employees Union President Robert Tobias against US Chamber of Commerce President Thomas J. Donohue, former Citibank manager Joseph J. Plumeri II, and Psychemedics President Raymond Kuacki, Jr., Donohue, a silver-haired, steel-blue-suited executive of the pre-60s breed, was introduced as a driving force behind the drug testing movement in the business community. He said that he had become concerned about debilitation of workers when he was a trucking company executive, but he offered no evidence that drug impairment was ever a problem. Tobias admitted that testing might be appropriate in some safety-sensitive positions, but insisted that it made no sense to be testing half the work
force. Strossen brilliantly impugned the efficacy of drug testing, invoking the ACLU's booklet by Lynn Zimmer and Dr. John Morgan, " Drug Testing: a Bad Investment. "
See
ACLU Report Urges End To Workplace Drug Tests; Government Says 70 Percent Of Drug Users Are Fully Employed

Strossen went on to say that drug testing too often detected off-the-job drug use that makes no difference to job performance. Donohue replied that it did make a difference, since people shouldn't be using drugs in the first place, and they might use them around their kids. His remarks provoked a disturbing round of applause from the audience.

Leslie Stahl chaired a panel on the entertainment industry and drugs.

Panelists deplored the glorification of drugs in movies like " American Beauty " and " The Beach, " while columnist Michael Medved scornfully noted that High Times was presenting its " Stoney Awards " later the same day.

Motion picture industry spokesman Jack Valenti defended the industry and the First Amendment with wit and aplomb.

FRIDAY: SHAKING HANDS WITH THE DRUG CZAR
Barry McCaffrey addressed the conference on the last day. He said nothing noteworthy or memorable.

A group of protesters, organized by Thousand Oaks activist Andrea Nagy, demonstrated against McCaffrey with signs and banners denouncing the drug war outside at the entrance to the driveway to the Reagan library.

As he was leaving the conference, McCaffrey happened to come face-to-face with me, so I shook his hand. I introduced myself as a sponsor of Prop. 215, and asked him to respect state's rights with regards to medical marijuana. " Well, thank you for your viewpoint, " he replied dryly.

The conference wound up with presentations by Partnership for a Drug-Free America Chairman James Burke and Robert Wood Johnson Foundation President Steven Schroeder, who expressed optimism about the future.

Burke presented slides showing how drug use had declined steadily during the 1980s, then leveled off and rebounded slightly in the 1990s. He noted that youth perceptions of marijuana risk had peaked around 1991, but then began to decline. He argued that the trend exactly paralleled the funding for the Partnership, which peaked at $350 million in 1991, but was down to $200 million in 1997. He cheerfully remarked that funding was being increased again under the new federal-private initiative, so there was reason to expect that drug use would once again decline.
See

and links

We left the Reagan Library having listened to voices from the past. Among them were a hard core of inveterate, long-time enemies like Burke, Donohue, Bennett and Meese, who were genuinely unapproachable. On the other hand, a good 25% of attendees seemed interested in reformist views, and many more were open to discussion. Among them was Califano himself, a charming man, with whom I had a pleasant exchange, thanking him for a stimulating conference with diverse viewpoints.

Dale Gieringer (415) 563-5858 // canorml@igc.org
